title: Penalties and Damages in Construction Contracts 2026
desc: What is the maximum contractual penalty in a construction contract and when can damages be claimed: Construction Law 2025, Civil Code and Commercial Law rules.
summary: Who decides the contractual penalty level, when it is capped at 8% or 12%, and how damages are calculated when a contractor is late or delivers poor quality.
body: p

A contractor delivering late, building contrary to the design, or a homeowner paying late are all breaches of contract. How far the injured party can claim a penalty or damages depends largely on what the two parties wrote into the contract, under Article 86 of the Construction Law 2025 and civil law.
h2
1. A penalty applies only if the contract provides for it
p

Under Clause 1, Article 86 of the Construction Law, bonuses, penalties and compensation for damage must be agreed by the parties in the contract. Article 418 of the Civil Code defines a contractual penalty as a sum paid by the breaching party to the injured party; the level is agreed by the parties unless the relevant law provides otherwise. If the contract has no penalty clause, no penalty can be claimed, only compensation for damage.
h2
2. What is the maximum penalty?
ul
Works under public-investment or PPP projects: the penalty must not exceed 12% of the value of the part of the contract that was breached (Clause 3, Article 86 of the Construction Law).

Contracts governed by the Commercial Law (between traders, or where a party not seeking profit, such as a homeowner, chooses to apply the Commercial Law under Clause 3, Article 1): the penalty or total penalties must be no more than 8% of the value of the breached part of the obligation (Article 301 of the Commercial Law).
Civil contracts between a homeowner and the person undertaking the work: the penalty level is agreed by the parties (Clause 2, Article 418 of the Civil Code).
p
Note: the penalty is calculated on the value of the breached part, not on the whole contract price, when the Construction Law (public investment) or the Commercial Law applies.
h2
3. Can you claim both a penalty and damages?
ul

Under Clause 3, Article 418 of the Civil Code: if the contract has a penalty but does not state that the breaching party pays both penalty and damages, the breaching party bears the penalty only. To claim both, the contract must say so expressly.
Under Article 307 of the Commercial Law: if a penalty has been agreed, the injured party may apply both the penalty and compensation.
For public investment and PPP, in addition to the penalty, the breaching party must also pay compensation as agreed (Clause 3, Article 86 of the Construction Law).
h2
4. How are damages calculated?
p

Compensation is determined by actual damage, or by pre-agreed levels of damage corresponding to the breached obligation (Clause 2, Article 86). The injured party may claim the benefits it should have obtained from the contract and the expenses arising because the other party did not perform its obligation (Article 419 of the Civil Code). Under the Commercial Law, there must be all of: a breach, actual damage, and the breach being the direct cause of the damage (Article 303).
p
Example: a contractor hands over the house late, forcing the homeowner to rent housing for 3 extra months; rent supported by invoices and a lease contract is actual damage that can be claimed.
h2
5. When is liability excused?
ul

Force majeure events: natural disaster, fire, epidemic, state of emergency, strike, discovery of antiquities, etc. (Clause 1, Article 13 of the Construction Law; Clause 2, Article 351 of the Civil Code).
A breach entirely caused by the other party's fault (Clause 3, Article 351; Article 294 of the Commercial Law).
If the breach is caused by a third party (for example a subcontractor or supplier), the breaching party remains liable to the other party (Clause 4, Article 86).
h2
6. Tips for drafting a penalty clause
ol
State each act that is penalised: schedule delay (penalty per day/week), poor quality, late payment.
State the maximum penalty and the basis of calculation (value of the breached work).
State clearly that the breaching party pays both the penalty and compensation for damage.
Agree on how a breach is notified in writing and the time to remedy it.
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The Commercial Law 2005 is partially no longer in effect; the articles cited are still in our library and should be cross-checked when signing a contract. When a dispute arises, consult a lawyer or a mediation centre.
